text: Thank you, Your Honor. Good morning, Chief Justice Rodriguez, Justice Palafox, and Judge Ferguson. May it please the court. I'm Thad Spaulding. I'm here on behalf of the appellants, Stephen Painter, and the families of Earl Wright and Albert Carrillo. We're back. This case has been here before. And we're back, although we're back in with some important distinctions from the last time we were here. Importantly, the original Painter case, as the court is well aware, dealt with vicarious liability of J.C. Burchette, who was a driller in this case and the driver at the time the accident occurred. This summary judgment that was granted is the third one that's been filed. It's the second time Amerimex has sought summary judgment on the basis of the workers' comp exclusion. First time it was denied. This time it was granted. And the workers' comp exclusion presents a different perspective on the facts as they pertain to course and scope. There's certainly some, as we learned from the Supreme Court in Painter, there's certainly some overlap between what the workers' comp law says and what the common law says. And there's not a significant amount of difference anymore. However, we do start with the general rule. And the general rule is that transportation to and from the workplace is not in the course and scope of employment. And that's what the passengers in this vehicle were doing at the time that the accident happened. They were traveling from the well site back to a bunkhouse that was in Fort Stockton. Now, under the statute, there's a couple of prongs. Some of the cases read it as three different prongs. But the first element is the court has to look at the nature of the activity and has to determine whether that activity, whatever the activity is, has to determine whether that activity relates to and originates in the business of the employer. And that's important because what we do know in the origination context is the same thing I said just a few minutes ago, which is that the general rule is travel to and from work does not originate in an employer's business. And why is that? The reason that is is because everybody, for the most part, has to travel to and from their job. And in doing so, you encounter the same risks that the general public encounters on their way to and from work. So there's got to be something more in order for travel to constitute, to have originated in the employee's business. And part of the problem with these comp cases and the origination element is all of the cases determine it's very fact intensive. And so you've got workers' comp cases and vicarious liability cases going back 60, 70 years with every possible permutation of facts. And what Ameramex has sought to do in this case, and really probably the reason that the summary judgment was granted in this case, is try and fashion a concrete rule. And in this case, they've tried to fashion that concrete rule out of the Seabright case from the Texas Supreme Court. And Ameramex has taken the position that these cases are on all fours. And so if they were in the course and scope for comp purposes in Seabright, they were definitely in the course and scope for our purposes here. That's not the case when you drill down, for lack of a better term, when you drill down, look at the evidence in this case and the particular circumstances in this case. So what we do know, let me back up a little bit, still kind of getting to what are the parameters we're working at? Not looking at specific facts of different cases, but what are the general rules that we can glean from some of these cases? And one of them is that ordinarily, the general rule is that transportation to and from work is not covered. Now, under some circumstances, transportation that is provided by the employer can be. But it's got to be a necessity from the standpoint of the employer, and it cannot be simply the gratuitous provision of transportation as an accommodation to the employees. And in this case, transportation was not a necessity from the standpoint of Ameramex. Now, Ameramex, this was a unique situation for Ameramex. And Mr. Murphree, who was Ameramex's chief financial officer, testified regarding this driller bonus that was provided as part of the contract between Sandridge and Ameramex. As Mr. Murphree testified, this was the only time they had ever done that. This is the only time they had ever paid this driver bonus. And the reason that they did it was because Sandridge wanted them to.

Of course, that never happened here. And so once they're in the Workers' Compensation Act, then we have to look to how the Act defines origination, and the Act looks to the activity, not to whether someone got paid. This dates back to the 1948 case of Ng, which the Texas Supreme Court quoted in our case and also in Seabright, I would recommend to the court. It's exactly like this. The passengers were not getting— nobody was getting paid for the time. The only thing they got was a mileage reimbursement back in the 80s. The same is true for Lopez.

speaker: ginapalafox
text: Even in Painter, the analysis then took that hard look at how you apply the analysis of course and scope objectively. And so from the point of view of the passengers, what are the objective factors that lead you to a conclusion that at the time they were acting in the course and scope of their employment?

speaker: karenburgess
text: The Workers' Compensation Act, which was not before the court in Painter. So in Painter, the court was reviewing it from a common law vicarious liability standard. Here, you have to go to the Workers' Compensation Act. And that's where the bar applies. And that's where Seabright is controlling. There, they said, and this is why Seabright and Amerimax are different than McDonald's, Justice Rodriguez. Because those businesses, and this is a quote from that case, call for employing specialized non-local work crews and constantly changing remote locations on temporary assignments. The employer was doing that, just like is true here and just like is true in Seabright and in Ng. Lopez wasn't paid for his time. Lopez had full control of where he wanted to stay. In fact, the dissent found that he was not within the course and scope under the Workers' Compensation Act because he did choose to stay in Marlin, 40 miles away. And they said, the dissent said, hey, you could have stayed much closer. There were other motels, but you chose to stay in this really remote place. And so your travel wasn't actually dictated by the nature of the business. Here, it's really important that the statute doesn't talk about who's doing what, unlike vicarious liability course and scope, where you do have to do that analysis of the individual and objectively look at what the facts are. In Seabright, what the court says is the ultimate inquiry is whether the relationship between the travel and the employment was so close that it can fairly be said that the injury had to do with and originated in the employer's business. And there can be no question under the facts of Ng and under the facts of Seabright that that is true here. You could also look at the Pasqueda case, exactly the same. I mean, these accidents happen coming from remote job sites to these bunk houses and other temporary shelters. And that's why the Comp Act is there, Justice Rodriguez. That's why the Comp Act doesn't pay for you to go home from your job at McDonald's. Yet it does say when the travel itself is necessitated by the nature of the work, like it is here, and it's provided for by the employer, then you're going to be within the Workers Compensation Act. That's why Mr. Lopez was within the Workers Compensation Act. That's why Mr. Ng was within the course and scope under the Workers Compensation Act.

speaker: yvonnerodriguez
text: Talk to us a little bit about the fact, and Mr. Murphy made this, I think, very clear, is that Ameramex did not pay for the transportation, and that the drivers would, you know, they would do some kind of bookkeeping or accounting, and then they would invoice Sandridge. And then once Sandridge paid Ameramex, then Ameramex would just then would forward that money to the drivers. And so his position was Ameramex never paid for any of this travel. Now, I understand that Mr. Perchette got a check from Ameramex, and that's a check to cash, but when you say it's paid for by the employer, I mean, that deposition makes it very clear that their chief financial officer of your company said they did not pay for transportation, and they weren't responsible for it. And if Sandridge didn't pay them the money, they weren't going to pay their drivers.

speaker: karenburgess
text: Justice, the statute says nothing at all about being reimbursed. In fact, if you were going to take that to its logical conclusion, all of our drilling costs were reimbursed by Sandridge. So, yes, labor was also reimbursed by Sandridge. Everything, Sandridge contractually required Ameramex to pay for that travel and to furnish that travel. Certainly, we cannot say that the workers themselves provided their travel that day. We can't say that Perchette provided their travel that day. He was paid for, he was paid by Ameramex, and Ameramex was reimbursed. That's not a fact question. We have, but there's case law, including the Bushman case out of San Antonio that we cited that gives, for instance, when an individual is using his own car and gets reimbursed, that still falls within the exceptions to the coming and going rule as a paid for transportation, and that's true here. I want to note on Seabright, the argument that you've heard about necessity, the word necessity is not in Seabright. The word necessity is not in Ng. The word gratuitous does show up because the defense tried to argue it in trying to avoid workers' compensation coverage, and because he wasn't required to have a truck, and he asked for a truck, and they gave him a truck. Still, that was not enough of a, that's the same sort of fact issue that you might come up with in the reimbursement, and yet that wasn't enough to create a fact issue that was material. The other issue, the other kind of fact issue that the talents would like to raise is this per diem question, and it's just a complete distinction without a difference because no matter who was paid a per diem, just without taking, you know, you don't need to know the facts on that. The facts are immaterial in that regard because there was no per diem in Ng at all. That didn't matter. All it was was a $0.07 per mile. It was 1948. $0.07 per mile reimbursement on the driving, and Seabright specifically talks about the per diem being to offset lodging. Well, here we gave them the lodging, and so they get the travel, they get the lodging, and so they're covered within the provisions of the Texas Workers' Compensation Act there. Amerimax, it's undisputed that Amerimax paid for both the travel and the lodging. The fact is that you just absolutely cannot distinguish Seabright. That business required the employees to stay in the temporary housing. The business required employees to stay in temporary housing. It wasn't Seabright that required something specific. The same is true here. Seabright didn't.

speaker: yvonnerodriguez
text: Amerimax doesn't require the crew members to stay in the bunkhouse.

speaker: karenburgess
text: Absolutely not. They can stay anywhere they'd like, and that's one of the things that the Texas Supreme Court said. We're not looking at what could have happened. We're looking at what did happen, and the court made that very clear. They're going to analyze this from what was happening that day, and they were undisputably traveling from the remote work site to the bunkhouse.

speaker: royferguson
text: I'm concerned about taking that one sentence in Seabright out of context because the sentence is that Interstate's business required its workers to obtain temporary housing and travel from the housing to the site. And so, yes, I mean that's a distinction in the language of the case, but do you think that's a factual distinction here between Interstate saying you've got to live closer to the site and in our case where Sandridge says we're going to give you a place to stay or Meramex, we're going to give you a temporary site, stay there, and we'll drive you back and forth?

speaker: karenburgess
text: Absolutely not. It's not a meaningful or material distinction. Not only has the court told us not to look at hypotheticals of what you could have done, but what you were doing. But secondly, it is exactly, as you said, the nature of the work that necessitates the remote. It's the nature of this remote work. What we need from the court- You have one minute. Just one minute warning. Sorry. Go ahead. Thank you, Justice. What we need from courts like you and what the Texas Supreme Court gave us back in Ng, where people were driving 450 miles from their houses in Big Spring to go work in Pecos and stay in Fort Stockton just like they're doing today, what the court gave us was a bright line rule. And they reminded us of that bright line rule in Seabright. And they said, if that travel is necessitated by the- it actually originates in the business of the employer, and that travel is furnished by, paid for, or controlled by the employer, which there's no question it was all of those things in this case, then that is going to be within the Workers' Compensation Act. And they need that bright line rule so they know which- is it Texas Mutual that's on the hook? Is it the carrier? Is it the employer who's on the hook? What is it? speaker: yvonnerodriguez
text: Thank you. Your time is up. All right. Miss- Mr. Spaulding.

speaker: thadspalding
text: Thank you, Your Honor. I take it to- I take it from that argument that the position now, and I don't think Seabright supports this, but the position now by AmeriMax is that work at any remote location, travel to that remote location is always going to fall within the course and scope of the employment, and that is not what Seabright says. And in fact, Seabright acknowledges that you have to look at the particular business and what they're doing and whether the travel is a- is an integral part of the work that is being performed. And what we do know from the history, and there's a long history of workers' comp cases in either- either in the comp context- or course and scope cases, either in the comp context or the vicarious liability context, what we do know is that just being out on a remote location is not enough. There's got to be more to it. And Seabright says- Seabright acknowledges that this was the nature of Interstate Treating's work, or at least the work that they were having Mr. Lopez perform, is he didn't come to the office in Odessa. You know, he was assigned to remote locations, to various remote locations. On this record, the Ameramex work was a one-off job. These guys were hired to come to the well, and they were only paid while they were at the well site. So when they got there, they started getting paid. When they left, they were no longer paid. Ameramex didn't care about the transportation. They were paying a bonus to a driller who would provide transportation, and it was his responsibility to take anybody that wanted to back and forth from the bunkhouse. But the crew members were not required to stay anywhere in particular. They could stay wherever they wanted to. And on this particular job, and if you look at the Fifth Circuit case in Rodriguez, where the employee was in Del Rio, or he was from San Antonio, he was working in Del Rio, and they required that he stay in Del Rio for four and a half days out of the week. They said, because his job was at a fixed location, and he was paid just for the time he was at that job, then the travel to and from that, even to and from San Antonio to Del Rio, that did not fall within the course and scope of his employment. Because the general rule has to be acknowledged here. And I think, Justice Rodriguez, you keyed on this, is that what Ameramex is arguing for is an exception that basically swallows the rule in any of these kind of situations. And it's an exception that travel to and from the work site is always going to fall within the course and scope of employment. They, there's a crucial distinction. And I disagree with Ms. Burgess on her interpretation of JANIC. JANIC is a dual purpose case. JANIC is not a, is not our situation. JANIC dealt with a situation where the driver and its crew members were on a, were going to get ICE for their job. And so they had varied from their ordinary route. They were on a, and the court determined that in going to get this ICE, they were doing, they were doing a task for their employer. They just weren't, it just wasn't going to and from work. And in that situation, they said it doesn't make sense to draw an imaginary line between the driver and the passengers, because the passengers are going to be part of that dual purpose too. And so we're going to lump all of them together. That's not the case here. You can draw a line. And in fact, the cases do, the painter does draw a line. You know, the line is, it doesn't expressly draw a line between the driver and the passengers because the passengers weren't at issue in, when the Supreme Court dealt with the vicarious liability of Burchett. What it did focus on is the fact that Burchett had a continuing obligation, a continuing duty on the part of his employer to transport employees. The fact that, the fact that we're in the workers comp context does not make a difference. This is not a benefit that any of the cases take into account in determining whether travel is a necessary, is a necessary element of, or falls with necessary element of the employer's business and therefore falls within the course and scope of employment. And, and the employee, you know, my client didn't waive their right to benefits. They, they were of the opinion, and they always have been, and we still are, that we aren't entitled to benefits under workers comp because we weren't in the course and scope of our employment. So that's why if you look at the workers comp decisions, which I think are persuasive, they're not, they're not binding, of course, but they are persuasive because workers comp appeals panels look at these cases all the time. And not that, not, not that this court doesn't, doesn't also, but I think the workers comp appeals panel looks at it a lot more than, than others. So I think it is persuasive when an appeals panel looks at these particular facts and, and even the appeals panel drew a distinction between what Mr. Burchett, the driller, was doing and his passengers who were not getting paid for any of their time and who were not obligated to stay at this bunkhouse. Ultimately, real quick, so I, so the, the fact that Ameramex wants to lump the two together, that legally, that falls apart. JANIC doesn't support it, and Liberty Mutual doesn't support it. In the Liberty Mutual case, you had the crew members were, the, the, the transportation was a part of their contract for the passengers. So there's a distinguishing feature in Liberty Mutual as well. But neither one of them stands for the proposition that you cannot differentiate between a driver who is paid and is obligated on behalf of the employer to drive crew members back and forth from the well site from crew members who are not getting paid, who are not getting reimbursed and who have no obligation to drive with the driller or stay in the bunkhouse and are not getting paid once they step off, once they step off the premises.

speaker: royferguson
text: Mr. Spaulding, that recitation of facts about the crew members is exactly the same recitation of facts in Seabright. Isn't that correct? It's exactly the same. They weren't required to stay there. They weren't required to drive. They weren't paid to go. They weren't on the clock and they were reimbursed. So there's no distinction between those two groups based on what you just said as the distinguishing characteristic. So, and by the way, it also doesn't say in Lopez and Seabright, it uses the word enabled by the benefit, enabled by providing per diem or in our case, $50 for the trip. Isn't that kind of what we have here? speaker: thadspalding
text: Okay. First, Judge Ferguson, first of all, with regard to Seabright, an important distinction, I think, and I agree with you that there was no requirement, although they were required to stay near the remote site, which is not the case here. Seabright did not address passengers. So if we're drawing a distinction, the passengers were not an issue in that case. Seabright involved Lopez, who had a company car, and whose job it was to go to these remote locations and complete the work. And he did it on numerous occasions. This particular one, at least my reading of the opinion, seems like it is consistent with what his job was throughout his time with interstate treating. The passengers in that case, we don't know about the passengers in that case. There were passengers there. We don't know if they were from the area. We don't know whether they were required to stay nearby or how they came to be. And so the facts between the two are distinguishable. With regard to the transportation, yeah, they could take the transportation, and they got free transportation. But what we do know from a legal standpoint is merely the gratuitous provision of transportation is not enough to put the travel to and from work in the course and scope of employment for origination purposes. And part of the problem with these cases is they kind of bleed, you know, you bleed an origination. And I think this gets to Ms. Burgess's argument, where I think she wants to make travel to and from work both an exception to the exclusion and part of the origination in the employer's business, which basically swallows the entire rule and completely ignores the distinction between origination, which must mean something different than, and must require a higher standard for establishing that travel, what we're talking about here, is a necessary part of the nature of the employer's business. And I think if you look at Murphy's testimony in that case, in this case, they were not concerned with not having a crew or not being able to get these guys out to the area because of transportation. Their concern, and this is the summary judgment context, and this is where fact issues arise, their concern was not paying the same bonuses that other guys were in the same area. So it really has, you know, if you're looking at conclusively establishing, like Amerimex wants to do here, conclusively establishing those facts, that hasn't happened here. And it's important to note, too, that in Seabright, Seabright is a summary judgment case, but it was a cross motion for summary judgment case. So you've got both sides moving for summary judgment, and, you know, in the cross motion context, you know, my thought is, you know, everybody's agreeing that here's what the facts are, and we just need to apply the law. That's not the case here. It's their burden to conclusively establish the different elements of the course and scope test, and they haven't done it. And so I'm not sure exactly how much time I have left.

speaker: yvonnerodriguez
text: A little over two minutes.

speaker: thadspalding
text: Okay, great. That gives me time to, I want to point out one other thing, and that is there seems to me to be a fundamental issue with Amerimex's argument. They want to put Burchette and the passengers in the same category. What we learned from Painter, and there are some statements made in Painter that are instructive, but the ultimate takeaway from Painter is that there are fact issues. And there are fact issues that prevented summary judgment from being granted. And that's the Supreme Court reversing a summary judgment in a vicarious liability course and scope context. I don't see Amerimex stipulating here or anywhere that Mr. Burchette was in the course and scope of his employment. And so if they're not going to stipulate, so presumably when we go back to the trial court, Amerimex is still going to be arguing that Burchette was outside the course and scope of his employment. And if they're going to do that, how can they at the same time argue that they have conclusively established that our crew members were inside the course and scope of employment? Amerimex can't have it both ways. There are fact issues. The law does not support the conclusive establishment of their defenses. And we'd ask that this court reverse the summary judgment that was granted and remand this case for trial.
